title: Clock skew causes refresh token revocation to be bypassed in Private and Dedicated nodes
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Summary: Several customers on Dedicated and Private deployments reported that recently revoked refresh tokens were still usable for up to 60s after revocation. This permitted single-account access after a supposed logout or key rotation. Impact is scoped to Private (VPC/on-prem) and Dedicated clusters where node clocks drift more than the control plane and where token revocation propagation and local validation interplay.

Observed behavior: Control plane records revoke events and publishes token IDs to the revocation pub/sub. Worker nodes subscribe and cache revocations for O(60s) before falling back to control-plane lookup in rare cases. With clock skew > 30s between control plane and workers the worker's validation logic (which compares token.exp and token.iat with local time plus leeway) accepted tokens that had been revoked because the local time made the token appear valid and the revocation cache TTL hadn't yet been refreshed due to transient pub/sub lag.

Why this is critical: Customers rely on immediate revocation for session termination, password resets, and key rotation. Accepting revoked tokens breaks compliance needs and allows short-lived unauthorized access in highly regulated workloads.

Reproduction steps (internal):
1) Stand up a Private deployment with worker nodes intentionally skewed +45s ahead of control plane (force via /etc/chrony or container time namespace).
2) Issue a refresh token via the API and confirm it exchanges to an access token.
3) Revoke the refresh token via the admin revoke endpoint. Control plane shows revoke event published.
4) Immediately attempt a refresh from a worker node: worker accepts the refresh and issues a new access token for ~30-90s window.

Root cause: Race between three systems plus reliance on local clock: (a) token validation uses local clock with permissive leeway, (b) revocation relies on eventual pub/sub propagation and a local cache TTL, (c) when node clock is ahead the combination allows tokens that are revoked on the control plane to still appear valid locally until revocation cache refresh. The real bug is the validation code trusting local 'now' for revocation checks without verifying revocation state atomically or using monotonic time source relative to the control plane.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Deployed hotfix to Dedicated control plane to reduce revocation cache TTL to 5s and to add a conservative hard-check path (worker will call control-plane revocation endpoint synchronously on revoke events) for nodes that report clock skew > 10s. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2841)
- Notified impacted customers and recommended temporary mitigation: enforce NTP/chrony sync on Private nodes and restart worker service if drift > 5s.

Proposed permanent fix (plan):
1) Make token validation revocation-resilient by consulting a short-lived signed revocation vector embedded in token validate handshake (design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SEC/Revocation+Vector+Design).
2) Update worker SDK to use control-plane canonical time for auth-critical checks when clock skew detected; fall back to monotonic counters for TTLs.
3) Add end-to-end test harness that simulates clock skew and validates revocation semantics across Dedicated/Private topologies.
4) Ship as a targeted private-2026.03+ runtime patch and then broader runtime-1.21 release.

Rollout plan:
- 2026-03-12: Emergency mitigation patch to Dedicated and Hosted control planes (completed).
- 2026-03-18: Ship worker-side deterministic validation changes to Dedicated test cluster.
- 2026-03-25: Private customer patch package + upgrade notes and automated pre-check script to detect clock skew.

Customers impacted (initial):
- AcmeHealth (Private, EU region) — reported incident 2026-03-09
- FinBridge (Dedicated) — reported 2026-03-10
- Two additional early adopters (on-call notified and triaged)

Monitoring & postmortem actions:
- Added a revocation-acceptance dashboard (tokens accepted after revocation events) to Console incident view.
- Create runbook step: if > 0.1% revocation-acceptance events in 5m window escalate to SRE and security.

Open questions:
- Is short-term synchronous control-plane check acceptable for high-throughput tenants? Need perf bench.
- Should we rely on signed revocation vectors or move to push-based per-tenant enforcement?

Next steps (owner: Mateo Ruiz):
- Finalize design doc and security review by 2026-03-14.
- Landing PR for worker validation changes by 2026-03-16.
- Coordinate Private customer upgrade windows and provide pre-check script by 2026-03-18.
